rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 10 compounds and locate critical peak pairs. A midrange temperature and moderate gradient duration provide a baseline for optimizing selectivity and run time.

All peaks have excess resolution in the scouting run, so double the gradient slope to reduce the time penalty. Keep the starting composition and temperature fixed to assess how much separation the critical cluster retains.

Use an intermediate gradient duration to recover resolution in the crowded middle cluster while keeping the last peak much earlier than in the scouting run. This brackets the tradeoff between the resolution loss at 10 minutes and the time penalty at 20 minutes.

The 14-minute gradient avoids the time penalty and leaves only one under-resolved pair. Increase temperature by 5 °C to test whether selectivity improves that pair while maintaining a short elution time.

The critical pair may be near an elution-order crossover at 45 °C; another 5 °C increase tests whether it separates on the other side. The remaining pairs have ample resolution, and faster elution should preserve the zero time penalty.

At 60 °C, the pair that crossed between 45 and 50 °C should separate further. Extend the gradient to 16 minutes to protect the neighboring gap that narrows with temperature, while targeting a last-peak time below 10 minutes.

Test the intermediate temperature to balance separation of the crossed middle pair against the neighboring pair that becomes crowded at 60 °C. The 14-minute gradient should retain a zero time penalty and may bring both critical gaps close to baseline resolution.

Slightly steepen the gradient at the best temperature to test whether the post-crossover critical pair clears R = 1.5. The neighboring pair has some resolution margin, and the shorter gradient should preserve the zero time penalty.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the R = 1.59 neighboring gap while aiming to keep the crossover pair above 1.5. This tests a nearby alternative that may retain the maximum CRF with a better-balanced resolution margin.

The maximum CRF is already attained; test a higher starting organic fraction as an alternative that may shorten elution while preserving full resolution. This probes starting-composition selectivity, since adjusting gradient slope alone left little margin above R = 1.5.

Lengthen the gradient to restore the neighboring gap lost at the higher starting composition. The crossover pair now has modest resolution headroom, so this combination may achieve maximum CRF with a more balanced separation margin.

Increase starting organic fraction and gradient duration together to seek additional selectivity margin around both critical pairs. This extends the successful trend from injection 11 while targeting elution within the zero-time-penalty window.

Extend the gradient by two minutes to improve the R = 1.41 gap, using the other critical pair’s resolution margin. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, potentially retaining maximum CRF with more separation margin than the earlier optimal methods.

Test a slightly shallower gradient near injection 13, which achieved maximum CRF with both critical resolutions at 1.70. This should improve the earlier critical gap while keeping the other above 1.5 and the last peak just below the time-penalty threshold.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 11 to map another maximum-score method with a shorter elution time than injections 13–14. The observed trends suggest both critical pairs should remain above R = 1.5 with no time penalty.

This gradient slope lies between injections 12 and 13 and should lift the earlier critical gap above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. It targets another maximum-CRF method with faster elution than injection 13.

Use a gradient slope between injections 10 and 11 to balance their two critical gaps. This should retain resolutions above 1.5 and zero time penalty, potentially matching maximum CRF with slightly earlier elution than injection 11.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 17 to balance its critical resolutions of 1.67 and 1.58 while shortening elution. The final organic fraction should still be sufficient for all compounds to elute, potentially preserving the maximum CRF.

Preserve injection 8’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the gradient earlier at lower organic content. Since its last peak eluted before this shortened gradient would end at the outlet, this method should retain the maximum CRF.

Use nearly the same gradient slope as injection 13, which gave balanced critical resolutions of 1.70, but end the gradient earlier at lower organic content. All peaks are expected to elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving maximum CRF and useful resolution margin.

Match injection 17’s gradient slope and starting composition while lowering the endpoint to 0.60. Its last peak eluted at 8.00 minutes, before this gradient ends at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, so the method should preserve full resolution and maximum CRF.

Preserve injection 19’s gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then test a lower-organic terminal hold. The critical separations should remain unchanged; this run checks whether the last compound still elutes within the zero-time-penalty window.

Use a slope close to injection 13’s to retain its balanced critical-pair resolution, then hold at 0.50 organic. This tests whether the lower endpoint still allows the last peak to elute before 10 minutes and preserves maximum CRF.

The maximum score is already secured; test whether a shallower gradient at 60 °C can restore the neighboring separation that limited injection 6. The higher starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak near the zero-time-penalty window.

Preserve injection 23’s gradient slope and temperature, which gave a minimum resolution of 1.69, but continue the gradient through the last peak instead of entering a hold. This should retain maximum CRF while reducing the last peak’s retention time and broadening.
